title: The Eastern Question
competency: Understand the nature of the Eastern Question, the role of nationalism in it, and the causes and consequences of the Balkan Wars.

keywords.def: What would happen to the Ottoman Empire's lands as its power declined (late 18th–early 20th c.).
The movement to unite the Slav peoples; in Serbia, a union of the southern Slavs.
A friendly understanding between states, short of a full alliance.
The 1912 alliance of Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria and Greece against the Ottomans.
The two wars of 1912 and 1913 in the Balkan Peninsula that took almost all of Europe from the Ottomans.

en.text: The Eastern Question was what would happen to the Ottoman Empire's lands as its power declined, from the late 18th to the early 20th century. Balkan national movements, usually backed by Russia, rose against the Ottomans, while Austria-Hungary and Britain wanted the empire preserved. After revolts in 1875–76 and the Reichstadt Agreement (July 1876), Russia declared war in April 1877. The Treaty of San Stefano (3 March 1878) favoured Russia, so the great powers revised it at Berlin (13 July 1878): Bulgaria was split and Austria got Bosnia and Herzegovina, which it annexed in 1908, angering Serbia.

screens.title: A weakening empire
screens.ask: A great empire is growing weak and its subject peoples want freedom. What do neighbouring great powers usually do?
opts: Compete to gain its lands or protect their interests
screens.after: This competition over the declining Ottoman Empire was the "Eastern Question".

The Ottomans crushed them by August 1876.

Austria-Hungary was to get Bosnia and Herzegovina.
April 1877: Russia declared war on the Ottoman Empire.
It used rumours of Ottoman atrocities as an excuse.
Russia then threatened Constantinople (Istanbul).
Britain, backed by Austria-Hungary, opposed Russia.

screens.title: Bosnia, 1908
paras: 1908: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Pan-Slav nationalists in Serbia were outraged.
They saw Bosnia as Serbian land, for a union of southern Slavs.
This became a long-term cause of World War I.
screens.note: The book calls it an "immediate cause"; the immediate cause was the Sarajevo assassination of 28 June 1914.

en.text: After 1878 Germany drew away from Russia and made the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary (1879). It grew close to the Ottoman Empire, reorganised its army and finances and won concessions such as the Baghdad Railway, which opened a route toward the British-controlled Persian Gulf. Rivalry with Britain and France grew. Britain settled its differences with France in the Entente Cordiale (1904) and with Russia in the Anglo-Russian Entente (1907).

ideas.name: The Balkan Wars and the road to 1914

en.text: In 1912 Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria and Greece formed the Balkan League, with Russian support, to take Macedonia. The First Balkan War began on 8 October 1912 and ended with the Treaty of London (30 May 1913): the Ottomans lost almost all of Europe and Albania became independent. The allies then quarrelled over Macedonia; Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece on 29–30 June 1913, lost to them, Romania and the Ottomans, and the Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913) gave most of Macedonia to Greece and Serbia. Austria-Serbia tension grew, and the killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 led to World War I.

screens.title: The First Balkan War
paras: Bulgaria, Greece, Montenegro and Serbia were already independent.
But many of their peoples still lived under Ottoman rule.
1912: they formed the Balkan League, with Russian support.
Aim: take Macedonia from Turkey.
8 October 1912: the war began; the allies soon won.
3 December 1912: armistice.
January 1913: a Young Turk coup in Constantinople restarted the war.
Ioánnina fell to Greece, Adrianople to Bulgaria.
Treaty of London (30 May 1913): the Ottomans lost almost all of Europe.
Albania became independent; Macedonia was to be divided.

screens.title: The Second Balkan War
paras: The allies quarrelled over dividing Macedonia.
Night of 29–30 June 1913: King Ferdinand of Bulgaria attacked Serbian and Greek forces.
Romania joined Serbia and Greece.
The Ottomans attacked too and regained Adrianople.
30 July: armistice. 10 August 1913: Treaty of Bucharest.
Greece and Serbia divided most of Macedonia.
Greece also gained Crete; Serbia gained Kosovo.
All sides committed grave atrocities against civilians.
The Ottomans kept only eastern Thrace (with Adrianople) and Constantinople in Europe.
screens.note: Albania was made independent by the great powers; in 1914 they gave it a German prince as ruler.

screens.title: The road to World War I
paras: Tension grew between Austria-Hungary and Serbia.
Serbia claimed Albanian land.
October 1913: Austria-Hungary, sure of German support, ordered Serbia out of the Albanian borderlands.
28 June 1914: Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
Franz Ferdinand was heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne.
This happened in Sarajevo, capital of Bosnia.
Austria-Hungary invaded Serbia, and World War I began.

notes.text: p.21: "Britain urged Austria and Germany to ally with it against Russia" is doubtful; Britain sent its fleet and threatened war, backed by Austria-Hungary, and Bismarck hosted the Congress of Berlin as "honest broker". Taught that way.

p.22: the 1908 Bosnia annexation is called "an immediate cause of World War I"; it is a long-term cause, the immediate cause being Sarajevo (28 June 1914). The Pan-Slav clause is garbled; read "who regarded Bosnia as Serbian land".
p.23: "Albania was made an independent state by a German prince" is garbled; the great powers made Albania independent (1912–13) and in 1914 placed the German prince Wilhelm of Wied on its throne.

p.24: the ultimatum to Serbia over Albania is usually dated 18 October 1913 (book: 17 October); the lesson says "October 1913". Franz Ferdinand was the Archduke and heir, not "the Austrian prince"; Princip was a Bosnian Serb.

Unit Summary says the Balkan Wars took "all" Ottoman territory in Europe; p.22 rightly excepts eastern Thrace and Adrianople. The Summary dates the Eastern Question "since the 1850s"; the lesson uses p.20 (late 18th–early 20th c.).
